title: Legal AI startup Harvey lands fresh $300 million in Sequoia-led round
author: Sharon Goldman

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The report supports Harvey as a significant test case for specialised legal-AI infrastructure: it documents substantial funding and company-reported commercial growth, while presenting contextual, interactive legal workflows and lawyer–engineer collaboration as Harvey’s differentiation. It appropriately treats revenue growth and investor enthusiasm as reported indicators rather than proof of accuracy, durable adoption or competitive advantage.
qs: In an exclusive interview with Fortune, Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg said the startup has surpassed $50 million in annual recurring revenue and estimated it would surpass $100 million ARR in about eight months.

"Legal work is incredibly complex and requires so much context, that a simple chatbot doesn't work," said Weinberg, who described his startup as developing a tool that offers suggestions and clarifications along the way, and allows lawyers to provide feedback about what they want.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source supports the cluster by documenting investor backing, company-reported revenue and elite-firm adoption, while presenting Harvey as an interactive, lawyer-informed application rather than a simple chatbot. It does not independently establish accuracy, productivity, intensive use or governance effectiveness, and clearly distinguishes current reported revenue from the CEO’s forecast.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the proposition that specialist legal application layers can retain value over general foundation models, chiefly through integrated lawyer–engineer collaboration, domain expertise and multi-model product development. It does not provide measured performance evidence or substantively address the cluster’s verified-copilot deployment claim.
qs: However, Weinberg argues that Harvey's focus on hiring lawyers as domain experts and integrating them with Harvey engineers, has helped them get the most out of the AI models they use (which besides OpenAI include Anthropic's Claude and models from Mistral and Xai).

"They're literally telling our engineers, like, we need to do that section and that section and that section and that section, they're explaining the process of how to actually create different work products."  ## A lawyer and a scientist team up  Weinberg's own inspiration for Harvey goes back to his experience a first-year associate at Los Angeles law firm O'Melveny in 2022.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source presents Harvey’s funding, revenue and customer growth as evidence of strong commercial traction while distinguishing reported results from forecasts and investor confidence. It also records the unresolved criticism that applications built on third-party models may lack durability, so it does not treat traction as proof of defensibility.
qs: In an exclusive interview with Fortune, Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg said the startup has surpassed $50 million in annual recurring revenue and estimated it would surpass $100 million ARR in about eight months.

However, after OpenAI's ChatGPT launched in November 2022, many critics dismissed Harvey-like startups as mere "GPT-wrappers": That is, those that did not develop their own AI models but used OpenAI's GPT-3, and then GPT-4 and beyond, to power their applications, would not last.

kp.k: Harvey funding reflects investor enthusiasm for enterprise legal AI
kp.d: Fortune reports that Harvey raised $300 million in a Sequoia-led Series D at a $3 billion valuation, double its July valuation. The article frames the financing as reflecting investor enthusiasm for AI applications gaining business customers. Other investors include OpenAI Startup Fund and REV, the venture capital arm of LexisNexis owner RELX Group.
qs: Harvey, a San Francisco AI startup focused on the legal industry, has raised $300 million in a funding round led by Sequoia that values the startup at $3 billion — double the amount investors valued it at in July.

The Series D funding round builds on the momentum of the three-year old startup, which was founded by a former lawyer and a Google AI researcher, and reflects investors' enthusiasm for AI tools that have succeeded in making inroads with business customers.

kp.k: Reported customer growth accompanies a revenue-doubling forecast
kp.d: CEO Winston Weinberg said Harvey had surpassed $50 million in annual recurring revenue and forecast surpassing $100 million ARR in about eight months from the February 2025 interview. Separately, the company reported expanding from 40 to 235 customers across 42 countries in 2024, including the majority of top 10 U.S. law firms. These are company-reported adoption and revenue figures, with the $100 million figure explicitly a prediction.
qs: In an exclusive interview with Fortune, Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg said the startup has surpassed $50 million in annual recurring revenue and estimated it would surpass $100 million ARR in about eight months.
In 2024, the company said it expanded from 40 customers to 235 customers in 42 countries, including the majority of top 10 U.S. law firms.

kp.k: Harvey supports research, contract analysis and document drafting
kp.d: The article describes Harvey as providing large-language-model tools to law firms and corporate legal teams. Weinberg argues that legal complexity and contextual demands require more than a simple chatbot; he describes an interactive tool offering suggestions and clarifications while allowing lawyers to provide feedback.
qs: Harvey uses large language models to help law firms and corporate legal teams streamline research, analyze contracts, and draft documents.

"Legal work is incredibly complex and requires so much context, that a simple chatbot doesn't work," said Weinberg, who described his startup as developing a tool that offers suggestions and clarifications along the way, and allows lawyers to provide feedback about what they want.

kp.k: Lawyer-engineer collaboration is Harvey's claimed product differentiator
kp.d: Weinberg attributes Harvey's ability to use AI models effectively to employing lawyers as domain experts alongside engineers. He says lawyers from large firms and in-house teams design and evaluate the product and explain the processes for creating legal work products. The article reports that Harvey uses models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral and Xai; the claimed advantage concerns domain-specific application development rather than exclusive reliance on one model provider.
qs: However, Weinberg argues that Harvey's focus on hiring lawyers as domain experts and integrating them with Harvey engineers, has helped them get the most out of the AI models they use (which besides OpenAI include Anthropic's Claude and models from Mistral and Xai).
"We have tons of lawyers on staff designing and evaluating the product, and they're all from large law firms or from large in-house teams," he said.

"They're literally telling our engineers, like, we need to do that section and that section and that section and that section, they're explaining the process of how to actually create different work products."

kp.k: Legal AI applications face a crowded competitive market
kp.d: Fortune identifies Casetext, Eve, Spellbook, Robin AI and Lex Machina as competitors in a crowded legal AI application market. It also notes incumbent ownership of Casetext by Thomson Reuters and Lex Machina by Lexis Nexis.
qs: The market for AI apps in the legal industry has become crowded, with competitors including Casetext (which was acquired by Thomson Reuters), Andreessen-backed Eve, Spellbook, Robin AI, and Lex Machina (owned by Lexis Nexis).

kp.k: Sequoia sees legal text workflows as generative AI opportunities
kp.d: Sequoia partner Pat Grady bases his investment thesis on the size of the legal market, which he puts at $400 billion in the U.S. alone, and its reliance on processing and reasoning over text. This is an investor's assessment of market opportunity and technological fit, rather than a measured finding about legal performance.
qs: Pat Grady, partner at Sequoia Capital, told Fortune that targeting the legal market with generative AI "kind of felt like a bulls-eye. For one thing, the industry is big — a $400 billion market in the U.S. alone. In addition, it felt like a good fit for the technology.
"A lot of what happens in the legal world is text in, text out, and it's reasoning over that text," he said.

kp.k: Investors contest predictions that model-dependent application startups cannot last
kp.d: The article reports critics' post-November 2022 argument that startups such as Harvey were merely GPT-wrappers and would not endure because they used external models rather than developing their own. Grady rejects that investment implication, saying Sequoia has continued investing in application companies. He also attributes confidence in Harvey's durability to Weinberg's development as a CEO and ability to build teams and an integrated company.
qs: However, after OpenAI's ChatGPT launched in November 2022, many critics dismissed Harvey-like startups as mere "GPT-wrappers": That is, those that did not develop their own AI models but used OpenAI's GPT-3, and then GPT-4 and beyond, to power their applications, would not last.
"We have been delighted to let that narrative persist," said Sequoia's Grady. "We've been loading up on application companies."
Seeing Weinberg grow into his CEO role, he added, gave Sequoia the confidence that "the machine is in place that will keep this company going for many years to come."

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article presents AI as assisting legal research, contract analysis and drafting, and reports rapid commercial adoption of Harvey. Weinberg attributes product effectiveness to context-sensitive interaction and lawyer–engineer collaboration; investor Pat Grady argues that legal work is well suited to generative AI.
pts.d: Goldman describes Harvey as a tool for streamlining work by law firms and corporate legal teams. Weinberg says a simple chatbot is insufficient for complex, context-dependent legal work and describes an interactive product that offers suggestions and clarifications while accepting lawyers' feedback. He argues that employing legal domain experts alongside engineers helps Harvey get more from third-party models. These are augmentation claims, not claims of autonomous lawyer replacement. On commercial expansion, Goldman reports a $300 million Series D at a $3 billion valuation, while Weinberg reports ARR above $50 million and predicts it will exceed $100 million in about eight months. The company reports growth from 40 to 235 customers during 2024. Grady grounds his investment thesis in the size and text-based nature of legal work and expresses confidence in Harvey's long-term durability despite criticism of application companies as 'GPT-wrappers.' The source makes no concrete prediction about lawyer job losses, billing models or access to justice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of company-reported adoption and revenue, reported financing, founder experience and product-development descriptions, and an investor's market thesis; no quantified legal-work performance results are supplied.
pts.d: Commercial traction is supported by the company's customer counts, geographic reach and penetration among top U.S. firms, the CEO's ARR statement, and the reported funding and valuation. These figures concern business growth rather than measured improvements in legal accuracy or productivity. Weinberg supports his product-design argument with descriptions of lawyers from large firms and in-house teams designing and evaluating the product alongside engineers. The founding story describes a GPT-3 prototype answering Reddit legal questions and outreach to OpenAI, including its then-general counsel, but supplies no test scores or systematic assessment. Grady offers an investor's assessment of a $400 billion U.S. legal market and the fit between generative AI and text-based reasoning. The article supplies no benchmark, time-saving measurement, error-rate study or client-outcome evidence for the streamlining claim, and no quantitative model underlying the ARR forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current capabilities and traction are described as of February 12, 2025; adoption figures cover 2024, and Weinberg's revenue forecast extends roughly eight months beyond the interview.
pts.d: The reported ARR above $50 million is a current CEO statement at publication. The forecast of more than $100 million ARR implies approximately October 2025, rather than an expressly named deadline. Customer growth from 40 to 235 is explicitly attributed to 2024. The valuation is reported as double the July valuation. The product argument is qualified by the complexity of legal work: Weinberg says useful assistance requires context, iterative lawyer feedback and domain experts translating work-product processes into engineering requirements, rather than a simple chatbot. Grady's expectation of durability extends to 'many years to come' without a precise horizon and is tied to his assessment of leadership and team-building. No deadline is given for profession-wide transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms and corporate legal teams using AI assistance, lawyers and engineers developing the tools, and legal-AI vendors and their investors competing for enterprise demand.
pts.d: Law firms and corporate legal teams are identified as users of assistance with research, contract analysis and document drafting; adoption evidence particularly highlights top U.S. firms, with customers across 42 countries. Lawyers remain involved through feedback, while lawyers hired from large firms and in-house teams contribute domain expertise to product design and evaluation. Harvey is presented as a software provider, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work. Goldman describes a crowded legal-AI application market including Casetext, Eve, Spellbook, Robin AI and Lex Machina; Harvey's funding and growth claims concern competition and investment in that vendor market. The article does not identify measured effects on end clients, smaller practices, the public, staffing levels or legal fees.
